analysis.one_liner: Requires retail electricity suppliers nationwide to meet a federal standard for renewable power.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 17, 2026, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy Committee, where it awaits action and has not received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend a 1978 federal utility law to create a national renewable electricity standard, forcing retail electricity suppliers across the country to supply a set share of their power from renewable sources like wind and solar. A federal standard of this kind would speed up renewable energy construction nationwide, replacing electricity now generated from fossil fuels. The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 17, 2026, and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee; it has one cosponsor and no committee action yet.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, consumers would benefit over time from a cleaner and potentially cheaper electricity mix as renewables scale up, and from reduced exposure to fuel price swings, since wind and solar have no fuel cost. Renewable developers, manufacturers, and construction workers in those industries would gain guaranteed national demand. People in communities with fossil-plant pollution would see cleaner air. States with their own weaker standards would see their utilities pulled up to the federal floor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renewable energy builders; ratepayers over time

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require retail electricity suppliers nationwide to meet a rising federal target for renewable power, accelerating wind and solar deployment under federal rules rather than leaving it to voluntary state programs.
By creating a single national market for renewable electricity credits, it would give utilities a uniform compliance path instead of a patchwork of state standards.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall first on utilities that own fossil-fired plants, which would have to buy renewable credits or build new capacity, and those costs would be passed through to electricity ratepayers, at least in the near term as fossil plants are retired before replacement infrastructure is fully in place. Regions dependent on coal, gas, and oil production would bear concentrated economic losses.

drawbacks.text: The CRS description is too sparse to establish the standard's timeline or stringency, so the compliance costs to utilities—and the electricity price increases that could pass through to ratepayers—cannot yet be judged.
A federal mandate overrides state choices about energy mix, and regions dependent on coal, gas, or oil jobs and tax bases would bear concentrated losses as those plants lose market share.

Renewable buildout requires transmission lines, permits, and critical minerals, all of which have lagged; a purchase mandate without those enablers could raise prices without delivering the clean energy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is lower long-term emissions and cheaper renewable power, but the bill carries real costs and objections: it raises near-term electricity prices as utilities replace reliable fossil plants, imposes federal mandates on states that have chosen their own energy mixes, and risks stranded costs in fossil-dependent regions. On the other side, a RES alone is a blunt tool; without transmission and permitting reform it may not deliver clean power fast enough. Whether the trade is worth it depends heavily on details (timelines, banking, alternative compliance payments) that are not yet visible in the record. The larger obstacle is political: a two-sponsor bill in a narrowly divided Senate has essentially no path.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on September 17, 2026, and nothing further has happened; with Congress sitting until early January 2027, it could still move but has no hearings or votes on record.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 17, 2026, by Senator Welch.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
It has one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no action in committee since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If it dies quietly, coal-, gas-, and oil-fired generators and utilities that would have faced federal compliance costs are better off, and states keep control over their own energy mixes. Nothing has been decided yet, so no one has gained or lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal renewable electricity standard.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsors so far are two Democrats (Welch and one cosponsor); no Republicans have signed on, and no one has opposed it on the record yet.

industries.note: A national purchase mandate creates guaranteed demand for wind and solar generation and the renewable energy credits sold alongside it. This is the industry the bill primarily serves.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and gas power producers
industries.note: Utilities that rely on fossil generation would have to buy credits or build renewables, shrinking the market share and revenue of coal- and gas-fired plants.
Utilities gain a compliance mechanism but bear the cost of meeting the standard, some of which would be passed to ratepayers as higher electricity prices during the transition.

analysis.trajectory: With only two sponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very unlikely to reach a Senate vote before this Congress ends on January 3, 2027; most bills referred to committee at this point in a session die without a hearing or vote.
